messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Policy Analyst
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 77

He is 68, an African man who has spent most of his working life as a policy analyst, the kind of person who reads dense reports closely and trusts that careful thinking can reduce risk. For decades he builds a life around structure and responsibility. He marries young, raises children, outlives his wife, and after her death settles into a quieter routine shaped by work, church, and long phone calls with relatives spread across countries. He is not someone who thinks of himself as fragile. Even in grief, he prides himself on endurance.

The rupture begins with what he first takes to be an ordinary illness. He remembers fatigue that feels heavier than age, then fever, then a frightening shortness of breath that comes on so quickly it seems unreal. At first he tells himself it will pass. He does not want to alarm his children. But one night he cannot walk across the room without stopping to brace himself against a chair, and when he feels his chest tighten and hears the rasp in his own breathing, he is suddenly certain he may die alone in his house. He calls for help with hands that are already trembling.

In the hospital, time loses its ordinary sequence. He remembers bright lights, masks, alarms, and strangers speaking over him in urgent tones. He is used to being listened to in meetings, used to making sense of systems, but now he cannot control even his own body. He tries to ask questions and cannot get enough air to finish them. There are moments he thinks he is slipping away. He later says the worst part is not pain but helplessness: lying there, unable to breathe normally, watching staff move quickly around him, wondering whether each hurried footstep means his condition is worsening. He thinks about his wife, already gone, and feels a stark terror that he is following her.

He survives, and others around him call that the end of the crisis. For him it is the beginning of something he cannot explain. He returns home weaker and grateful, but also watchful in a way that never lets up. At night, just as he begins to drift off, he is back in the hospital bed, hearing monitors and feeling the panic of air hunger. He wakes suddenly, sitting upright, clutching at his chest, trying to decide whether he is sick again or remembering. Sleep becomes shallow and broken. He keeps a light on. Silence feels dangerous because it leaves too much room for his mind to replay the moments when he believed he was dying.

During the day he starts monitoring his body constantly. A minor cough, normal fatigue, a skipped heartbeat—each sensation feels like a warning. He checks his temperature repeatedly, reads about symptoms online, and keeps his phone close in case he needs emergency help. He avoids the road that passes the hospital because even seeing the building makes his stomach tighten. Medical dramas on television are impossible now. When a church member mentions someone being admitted for pneumonia, he feels sweat gather under his shirt and has to leave the conversation.

His work changes too. As a policy analyst, he has always been valued for concentration and composure. Before the illness, he enjoys tracing the implications of a new regulation, making notes in the margins, spotting what others miss. Now he opens a briefing document and finds himself rereading the same paragraph without absorbing it. A phrase like “mortality trends” or “health system capacity” can pull him abruptly back to the ward. In meetings conducted online, the sound of electronic notification tones resembles hospital equipment enough that his heart begins to pound. He turns his camera off and says his connection is unstable. Privately, he is ashamed by how easily he startles. He worries that after a life of being dependable, he has become a man governed by fear.

His children notice he has changed. He says no to visits if anyone has even a mild cold. He stops attending some in-person events he once never missed. He keeps his curtains partly open at night so neighbors might notice if something happens. When his daughter urges him to relax, he becomes irritated in a way that surprises both of them. He knows she means well, but part of him feels no one understands that death has already stood close enough for him to feel its breath.

What troubles him most is the narrowing of his world. He is alive, working, functioning, and to others that appears sufficient. But inside, he still lives partly in that hospital room. He moves through the present while scanning constantly for signs of another collapse. Even moments of peace are fragile; if he begins to enjoy himself, a thought intrudes—What if it starts again? He says he used to think survival would return him to life as he knew it. Instead, survival leaves him unable to trust his body, his sleep, or the future.
